note: Agreed fact/interpretation split. Where the two independent labelers (Sonnet, Opus) agreed, their label stands. Every disagreement was ruled by Varun on 2026-09-15 against the source excerpt. This file is an answer key: it says what KIND each clause is, never whether it is true.

why.text: Your MCP servers become ordinary stateless web services —
horizontal scale behind a plain load balancer, no sticky sessions, no shared session store.
The cost is a hard migration:
cross-version compatibility breaks, and Roots, Sampling, Logging, and Dynamic Client Registration are all deprecated on a 12-month clock,
so anything you built on those needs a replacement designed now.

example.text: If your agent's tool server relied on Sampling to call back into the model mid-tool,
— you have 12 months to restructure it as a request the client initiates.
And because compatibility breaks across versions, a client pinned to the old spec cannot talk to a new server,
so you run both fleets during the cutover rather than upgrading in place.

connection.text: Directly reinforces Terminal-Bench 2.1: with a 0.4-point gap at the frontier, the harness — transport, scaling, tool surface — is where your differentiation actually lives, and it just got rewritten.

why.text: 2.8T open weights at 1M context shifts build-vs-buy for agents, because per-call cost compounds across many calls per task
and self-hosting caps that cost. The tradeoff is blunt: you take on serving cost and latency to escape API pricing.

example.text: For an agent making 20 calls per task, the per-call price is multiplied by 20 before you see any value — the case for owning the weights.
you now pay that 20× in your own serving infrastructure and latency budget instead of someone's API line item.

connection.text: Cuts against the OpenAI/Anthropic mega-rounds: those ~$1T valuations set the pricing umbrella for API and talent, and open weights at this scale are the main lever a downstream builder has against it.

example.text: On a multi-turn task, outcome-only reward gives one signal for a whole trajectory; iStar scores each intermediate action instead,
so a run that took the right first three steps and failed on the fourth still teaches something. That per-step scoring function is the part you have to design yourself.

connection.text: Pairs with the MCP spec change: step-level credit assignment assumes you can cleanly attribute each tool call, which is easier when transport is stateless request/response than when state hides in a session.

ninety.method.text: Assign per-step implicit rewards so the agent gets credit on intermediate actions instead of only on the final outcome in multi-turn agentic RL.

ninety.result.text: +6.3% success improvement on WebShop and VisualSokoban.

ninety.caveat.text: Benchmark-only results, and the authors concede the difficulty concentrates in step-reward design
— the part you'd have to build for your own task.

why.text: A 0.4-point spread between GPT-5.6 Sol at 89.5% and Opus 5 at 89.1%
means model choice is no longer the variable that decides whether your coding agent works.
Differentiation moves to the harness and the eval design around it
— which is a harder, slower kind of engineering than swapping a model string.

example.text: Swapping between the top two models buys you 0.4 points; a better retry policy or tool schema in your harness plausibly moves more. Budget your quarter accordingly — spend it on the scaffold and your own evals, not on frontier benchmarking.

connection.text: Sets up the MCP item: if the harness is the differentiator, the 2026-07-28 transport change is the most consequential engineering item of the day.

why.text: OpenAI's $122B round at $852B post and Anthropic at $965B set the pricing umbrella
you build under
— it moves both API pricing
and what you pay for talent. If you're planning a company, both of your main input costs are being repriced by people who are not your competitors.

connection.text: Read with Kimi K3: open weights at 2.8T parameters are the only real hedge against a pricing umbrella set at ~$1T valuations.

why.text: $510B in H1 with AI taking ~80% of Q1 dollars
means an AI-labeled company raises into valuations priced for perfection — funding is available, but so is the expectation that you grow into it.
Anything not AI-labeled is fighting over the remaining ~20%.

connection.text: Same direction as the OpenAI/Anthropic rounds — capital concentration and frontier valuations are one phenomenon, and it prices your inputs before you write a line of code.

why.text: Chip access turns into a policy variable: Blackwell-class exports banned, H200 moved to case-by-case licensing.
That makes vendor and region choices contingent on where you and your customers operate, not just on price and availability.

connection.text: Tightens the Kimi K3 tradeoff — self-hosting a 2.8T open-weight model assumes you can get and keep the accelerators, and case-by-case H200 licensing makes that assumption jurisdiction-dependent.

thread.text: The frontier stopped being the differentiator on the same day it got the most expensive:

GPT-5.6 Sol beats Opus 5 by 0.4 points on Terminal-Bench 2.1 while OpenAI and Anthropic price at $852B and $965B, and AI absorbs ~80% of Q1 venture dollars. If the top two coding agents are a near-tie,
your leverage moves to harness and eval design — which is exactly what the 2026-07-28 MCP spec forces you to rebuild,
trading stateful sessions for stateless horizontal scale and a broken-compatibility migration.
Kimi K3's 2.8T open weights and iStar's step-reward credit assignment
both argue you can own more of the stack,
while trillion-dollar rounds and the AI OVERWATCH Act's Blackwell ban
argue the inputs — capital, talent, chips — are consolidating out of reach. Read that as a mandate to spend the next quarter on plumbing and evals, not on model selection.
